marrow__ANAT_CH25_Q001.takeaway: The middle/posterior lobe is the largest cerebellar lobe and coordinates balance and gait.
marrow__ANAT_CH25_Q001.displayText: The scenario is post-traumatic cerebellar ataxia with impaired balance; the gait image shows tandem-walk difficulty, poor heel-toe coordination, erratic foot placement and truncal sway. The largest cerebellar lobe is the middle (posterior) lobe, inferior to the primary fissure. The cerebellum has right and left hemispheres joined by the vermis and is divided into anterior lobe above the primary fissure, middle/posterior lobe below it, and flocculonodular lobe behind the uvulonodular fissure. Superior and inferior surfaces are separated by the horizontal fissure. Three cerebellar peduncles connect it with the nervous system.

rationales.a: The anterior lobe is smaller and lies above the primary fissure; the source identifies the middle/posterior lobe as largest.
rationales.c: The flocculonodular lobe is a small vestibular lobe behind the uvulonodular fissure.
rationales.d: Vermis is the midline bridge between hemispheres, not one of the three cerebellar lobes.

reconstruction.sourceFragment:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of post-traumatic cerebellar ataxia presenting with
impaired balance. The largest part of the affected structure i.e. the cerebellum is the middle lobe,
also known as the posterior lobe. The gait shown in the above video is a cerebellar ataxic
gait. Here, the patient is seen attempting tandem walking and displaying improper heel-toe
coordination, erratic foot placement, and truncal swaying.
The cerebellum consists of two hemispheres (right and left) joined by a median vermis. It is
divided into three lobes:
+ Anterior lobe - lies superiorly above the primary fissure
+ Middle lobe - lies inferiorly below the primary fissure
+ Flocculonodular lobe - lies posterior to the uvulonodular fissure
It has two surfaces, superior and inferior, separated by a horizontal fissure. It is connected to the
other parts of the central nervous system via three peduncles.

marrow__ANAT_CH25_Q003.takeaway: Vestibulocerebellar output centers on the fastigial nucleus.
marrow__ANAT_CH25_Q003.displayText: The oldest cerebellar component is the archicerebellum (vestibulocerebellum). It is associated with the fastigial nucleus, which connects through descending pathways with vestibular nuclei and medullary/pontine reticular formation.

rationales.b: Globose is an interposed deep nucleus and is not the phylogenetically oldest vestibular component.
rationales.c: Emboliform is also interposed; the oldest vestibulocerebellar part relates to fastigial output.
rationales.d: Dentate is associated with the newer cerebrocerebellum, not the oldest archicerebellum.

marrow__ANAT_CH25_Q005.takeaway: Granule cells are the only excitatory neurons of cerebellar cortex.
marrow__ANAT_CH25_Q005.displayText:
Ataxia-telangiectasia is characterized by progressive neuronal degeneration with a loss of Purkinje
and granule cells in the cerebellum. The granule cells are the only excitatory cells in the cerebellar
cortex.

rationales.a: Golgi cells are inhibitory interneurons, unlike excitatory granule cells.
rationales.b: Purkinje cells are inhibitory output neurons, not the excitatory cell type asked for.
rationales.c: Basket cells are inhibitory molecular-layer interneurons.

marrow__ANAT_CH25_Q006.takeaway: Purkinje cells are the sole output cells of cerebellar cortex.
marrow__ANAT_CH25_Q006.displayText:
The tremors are caused due to progressive degeneration of the Purkinje cells that form the output
of the cerebellar cortex. They form the only output neurons of the cerebellar cortex.
The output of the whole cerebellum is from the deep cerebellar nuclei namely fastigial, globose,
emboliform and dentate.
emphasis: only output neurons of the cerebellar cortex

rationales.a: Deep cerebellar nuclei are the output of the whole cerebellum, but not the sole output neurons of its cortex.
rationales.c: Granule cells are excitatory input-layer neurons and project parallel fibers; they are not cortex output cells.
rationales.d: Stellate cells are inhibitory interneurons in molecular layer, not the cortical output neurons.

marrow__ANAT_CH25_Q009.takeaway: Climbing fibers arise from the contralateral inferior olive and excite cerebellar circuitry.
marrow__ANAT_CH25_Q009.displayText:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of acute viral cerebellitis secondary to COVID-19. The true
statement regarding the cerebellar circuitry is that that all climbing fibres originate from the
contralateral inferior olivary nucleus.

Option A: Climbing and mossy fibers are excitatory and use glutamate and aspartate as the
neurotransmitters.
Option B: Mossy fibers terminate on the granule cells forming glomeruli.
Option D: Efferents of the cerebellum pass through the superior and inferior cerebellar peduncles.

rationales.a: Both climbing and mossy fibers are excitatory and use glutamate/aspartate rather than GABA.
rationales.b: Mossy fibers terminate on granule cells within glomeruli, not directly on Purkinje dendrites.
rationales.d: Cerebellar efferents use superior and inferior peduncles; not all leave only through superior peduncle.

rationales.d: Olivocerebellar fibers also enter through the inferior peduncle; anterior spinocerebellar tract enters superiorly and is the exception.

marrow__ANAT_CH25_Q013.takeaway: Superior peduncle carries major deep-nuclear efferents to red nucleus and thalamus.
marrow__ANAT_CH25_Q013.displayText: The highlighted structure is the superior cerebellar peduncle. It carries efferents from dentate, emboliform and globose nuclei, plus a smaller fastigial fascicle; fibers decussate in caudal midbrain and reach the contralateral red nucleus and thalamus. It also contains ventral spinocerebellar fibers. The middle peduncle carries afferents from contralateral pontine nuclei; the inferior peduncle carries brainstem/spinal afferents and efferents to vestibular nuclei.

rationales.a: Fastigial nucleus contributes a small efferent fascicle but is not the principal target asked for in the source item.
rationales.b: Inferior olive gives rise to climbing-fiber afferents rather than the superior-peduncle efferent destination.
rationales.d: Subthalamus is not the target identified for superior-peduncle output in the source.

reconstruction.sourceFragment:
The peduncle highlighted in the image is the superior cerebellar peduncle. The superior cerebellar
peduncle includes fibers from deep cerebellar nuclei that project to the brainstem, red nucleus,
and thalamus. It also contains the ventral spinocerebellar tract fibers.
The superior cerebellar peduncle contains all the efferent fibers from the dentate, emboliform,
and the globose nuclei, and a small fascicle from the fastigial nucleus. Its fibers decussate in the
caudal mesencephalon and are destined to synapse in the contralateral red nucleus and
thalamus. The middle cerebellar peduncle contains only afferent fibers from the contralateral
pontine nuclei. The inferior cerebellar peduncle is a mixture of afferent fibers from the brainstem
and spinal cord and efferent fibers to the vestibular nuclei.

marrow__ANAT_CH25_Q014.takeaway: Superior cerebellar artery ischemia may present with ataxia and incoordination.
marrow__ANAT_CH25_Q014.displayText:
Thrombosis of the superior cerebellar artery causes cerebellar lesion which presents with ataxia
and incoordination.
Blood supply of cerebellum:
+ Superior cerebellar artery
+ Posterior inferior cerebellar artery
+ Anterior inferior cerebellar artery

rationales.a: Posterior cerebral artery supplies occipital/temporal regions rather than the cerebellar artery named.
rationales.b: Middle cerebral artery supplies lateral cerebral hemisphere, not cerebellum.
rationales.c: Internal carotid supplies anterior circulation and is not a cerebellar artery.
